the-factory.title: The Mills
the-factory.summary: A demo booking and admin app for an event venue, built for my own practice. It covers bookings, payments and role-based access.

sections.heading: Who uses it
sections.body:
This is a demo app for an event venue. I built it for myself to practice and test ideas. It is not used by a real venue.

It has four staff roles: admin, manager, developer and viewer.

sections.heading: Why I built it
sections.body:
Some venue software is too hard to use. I wanted something simpler, with one place to see events, make bookings, check the calendar and find clients.

I also wanted a real project to learn Astro and practice full-stack work.

sections.heading: What I built
sections.body:
A two-step booking form that checks the details before it saves.

A dashboard with money by month, money by event type and upcoming events.

A calendar that shows paid, partly paid or unpaid events.

Roles that limit what each person can change. The server enforces this, not only the screen.

A read-only public view. Other pages need an access code.

sections.heading: Choices I made
sections.body:
Astro, because most pages only show data. React, only where a page needs interaction.

Cloudflare Workers runs the app, D1 is the database, and Sanity stores the venue data.

The server builds each booking, so the form cannot change the price.

sections.heading: What I fixed after testing
sections.body:
A fake cookie got into the admin area. I fixed it by signing sessions with HMAC.

Sign-in failed on Cloudflare because secrets were not readable at runtime. I turned on runtime access.

I learned that working locally does not mean it will work in production.

sections.heading: Testing
sections.body:
I ran 19 unit tests with Vitest, and none failed.

I ran Playwright browser tests at desktop and phone sizes. The last full run had two failures. I fixed both and ran it again.

sections.heading: Still to do
sections.body: Color contrast still fails on many pages. Invite and reset emails need an email key. I deploy by hand with Wrangler.

showcard.title: SHOWCARD
showcard.summary: A card app for Deaf and hard-of-hearing people. Save the messages you use most and show them in large text with one tap.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body:
ShowCard is a card app for Deaf and hard-of-hearing people. You save the messages you use most, like a doctor visit or a coffee order. When you need to say something, you tap a card and the message shows in large text for the other person to read.

I designed it, built it and tested it on my own.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body: Typing the same message over and over is slow, and harder during a medical visit or an emergency. Sometimes you just need to show a message fast, without speaking.

sections.heading: What I did
sections.body: I created the whole product, including the product and interaction design, the responsive interface, accessibility improvements, private-card security and encryption, automated unit and browser tests, and the documentation.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.body:
You make your own cards and show any card full screen. You can sort cards into groups, and emergency cards are easy to reach. There is a quick-write option for a one-time message.

Private cards are locked with a six-digit code, with a one-time backup key if you forget it. You can change the text size and pick light, dark or high-contrast colors.

sections.heading: Privacy
sections.body:
Private cards are encrypted before they are saved. I don't store the six-digit code. I store a derived hash, and a random key protects the data. After too many wrong codes, the app locks for a short time.

A six-digit code is short, so if someone gets a copy of the browser data, they could try to guess it. I want to be clear about that limit.

sections.heading: How I tested it
sections.body:
I tested it as a responsive web app. Playwright checked the features, the error messages, phone-sized layouts, keyboard use and accessibility. Vitest covered the unit tests.

I have not tested it with Expo or Xcode. It is a web app, not a native iPhone app, so I have not tried it on a real iPhone yet.

sections.heading: What was hard
sections.body:
Keeping private data safe without making sign-in confusing. I kept the code separate from the encryption key, so changing the code doesn't mean re-encrypting every private card.

The automatic accessibility tests found real problems, but I still need to test with real users and real phones.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.body: Test with Deaf and hard-of-hearing people, and with screen readers on a real iPhone and Android phone. Make it installable and work offline. Decide whether to build a native app with Expo or wrap this one with Capacitor.

chromatique.title: CHROMATIQUE
chromatique.summary: A tool for testing a text color and a background color before you use them in code. It shows WCAG and APCA contrast side by side, with a live preview and exports to CSS, Tailwind and design tokens.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body:
Picking a text color and a background color is easy to get wrong. A pair can look fine on my screen and still be hard to read for someone else.

WCAG and APCA also disagree. WCAG can pass some pale pairs that read badly. APCA tracks how people see lightness, but most tools don't show it next to WCAG.

sections.heading: What I built
sections.body:
Chromatique Studio is a tool for testing two colors before they go into code. You enter a surface color and a text color, and it shows both checks side by side.

The preview uses the same two colors, and you can edit the text to try your own copy. There are color-blindness previews, a shade scale, saved pairs and exports to CSS, Tailwind and design tokens. The current pair goes in the URL, so a link opens the same colors.

sections.heading: Why I show both checks
sections.body: I didn't want to pick a winner. The useful part is where the two checks agree and where they split. If a pair passes one and fails the other, you should stop and look.

sections.heading: How I built it
sections.body:
It's Vue 3 with the Composition API. The color state and the contrast math live in one composable, so I could test the math without opening the UI.

I also laid the tool out on one card, so a laptop and an iPad fit the screen with no scrolling.

sections.heading: Testing
sections.body:
I ran 30 unit tests with Vitest, and none failed. I ran 16 browser tests with Playwright, including axe scans on every preset and color-blindness mode, and none failed.

Lighthouse on the live build scores 100 for performance, accessibility, best practices and SEO.

sections.heading: What went wrong
sections.body:
Playwright was quietly testing another project, because both used the same port. Moving it to its own port fixed that.

My APCA score for black on white was 114, but the reference is 106. The unit test caught it.

A hint at 95 percent opacity dropped the red below AA contrast. Removing the opacity fixed it.

The scans ran during a color fade and read blended colors. They now wait for the final color.

sections.heading: Next
sections.body: I want an accent color with suggestions that already pass contrast, component tests for the Vue parts, and a manual screen-reader pass. Automated checks miss reading order and meaning.

09labs.title: 09 Labs
09labs.summary: A snippet vault and small design system. Keep your code snippets in one place, group them, and switch between three color themes.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body:
09 Labs is a snippet vault and a small design system. You keep code snippets in one place, group them, and switch between three color themes.

It starts with 35 snippets across about 20 categories. Your own snippets are saved in your browser, and there is no server.

sections.heading: Why I built it
sections.body: I kept rebuilding the same navigation, modals, cards and form controls for each project. I wanted one set of parts I could reuse, and a place for the snippets I use most.

sections.heading: Saving your snippets
sections.body:
You can create, edit and delete your own snippets. They are stored separately from the starter set, so the starter snippets are never overwritten.

If the browser blocks storage, the app logs the error and keeps running.

sections.heading: Themes and mobile
sections.body:
The three themes are light, coffee and dark. Each one is a set of CSS variables. The dark theme first failed contrast, so I gave accent backgrounds their own text color.

On a laptop the categories stay in a sidebar. On a phone they open in a drawer, with a row of pills across the top.

sections.heading: Search
sections.body: Search checks the title, description and tags, and it respects the category and Favorites filters. Cmd+K opens a command palette, and Ctrl+K does the same on Windows and Linux.

sections.heading: Sandbox
sections.body: The sandbox runs the code you type with eval, directly in the page. That means it can reach the page and the saved data. This is the next thing I need to fix. The plan is an iframe with no access to the page's storage.

sections.heading: Testing
sections.body: The public repo does not have automated tests yet. ESLint is set up, and the lint script runs on the whole project. I'm adding tests next, and I'll publish the numbers when they are in the repo.

sections.heading: Next
sections.body: The theme can flash the wrong color on load, because the saved theme is applied after the page mounts. Starter snippet edits only last for the session. Sidebar.tsx is about 755 lines and I would split it up.

vantage.title: VANTGE
vantage.summary: A web app for hosting an event. A host shares a photo gallery and an invitation through one link or QR code, and runs everything from one dashboard.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
Try the demo at vantge.app/try. The access code is Demo.

Vantge is a web app for hosting an event. A host shares a photo gallery and an invitation through one link or QR code, and runs everything from one dashboard.

I designed and built the host dashboard, the guest pages, and a browser-only demo.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body: Hosts use several tools for one event, and guests have to remember several links. I wanted one event with one link.

sections.heading: What I built
sections.body:
A live preview that updates as the host types or picks a color, font or background.

A background photo for each screen size: portrait for phones, landscape for desktop.

Guest pages that match the preview, with photo upload and a gallery.

The demo at /try uses sample data. Edits stay in the browser, and nothing reaches the live database.

sections.heading: Key decisions
sections.body:
The demo uses an in-browser stand-in for the database, so it is safe to share and easy to reset.

The preview stays beside the settings while you scroll.

Each page loads only when it is opened. The home page bundle went from about 930KB to about 225KB.

sections.heading: Testing
sections.body:
I ran 6 unit tests with Vitest, and none failed.

I ran Playwright with axe on the home and login pages. The scans found 15 low-contrast text problems, which I fixed.

I checked 5 pages at 360, 390 and 430 pixels. None scrolled sideways.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body:
A visitor can go from the start page to a styled event dashboard in three steps.

On the live build, the home page scores 100 on accessibility, best practices and SEO. I have not measured real visitor numbers yet.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.body:
The access code is Demo, at vantge.app/try.

I want to cut the JavaScript still loaded on the demo page, and measure how long a new host takes to create an event with real users.

kanso.title: KANSO
kanso.summary: A writing app with no dashboard and no big toolbar. Just a page and the few tools you need to write.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Kanso is a writing app for focus. There is no dashboard and no big toolbar, just a page and the few tools you need to write. It is React and TypeScript, with no backend, so your work stays in the browser.

sections.heading: The problem I fixed first
sections.body: The sidebar had two close controls. The header button opened it, but once it was open, the close button moved inside the panel, so it was hard to find. I wanted one button in the header that works in both states.

sections.heading: What I changed
sections.body:
The header button now opens and closes the sidebar, and its label and icon change with the state. I removed the second close button.

I added a pen logo beside the KANSO name. I also replaced the favicon with the same pen.

The accessibility scan flagged the small sidebar labels, so I raised their opacity from 40 or 50 percent to 70 percent. It took three rounds, because the first change missed some label styles.

sections.heading: Tests
sections.body: I used Vitest for unit tests on the header button, and Playwright for browser tests on desktop and phone sizes. Each browser run also runs an axe scan, with the sidebar open and closed. The tests work whether the saved setting opens or closes the sidebar.

sections.heading: The build that was failing
sections.body: The production build was failing before I started. A Vite setting was written in a form this version rejects, and Vercel would have failed the same way. I changed it, and the build passes.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: Vitest passes 2 of 2 tests and Playwright passes 6 of 6, including the axe scans. Lint is clean, and the live site scores 100 in all four Lighthouse categories. The dev server scores lower, because it doesn't bundle the code.

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.body: Run the same build command the host runs before merging. Measure the live site, not the dev server. When you change a color, search for the color itself, not one class name. And check small icons at their real size, since the pen's details disappeared at 32 pixels.

monolith.title: MONOLITH
monolith.summary: A small online store built in a three-step process: layout, accent colors, and animation.

sections.heading: How I built it, in three steps
sections.body:
I built Monolith in three steps: the layout first, then the accent colors, then the animation.

First I built the layout in grayscale. I wanted the grid, the spacing and the section order to work before anything looked finished.

Then I added the accent color on top of that base. I did not use color to fix a layout that wasn't working yet.

Last, I added the animation, so it would not hide problems in the layout or the colors.

The hardest part was not jumping ahead. As a designer, I wanted to add color and motion early. The three looks in the header come from these steps: grayscale, color and animated.

quality-lab.title: Quality Lab
quality-lab.summary: One dashboard that shows the latest automated test results for my apps, so I can see at a glance whether each one still works.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body:
I build several small apps. Each one has automated tests that run in GitHub Actions. The tests were working, but I had to open each project's GitHub page to see whether it passed.

I wanted one page that shows the state of every project.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.body:
Quality Lab reads the latest GitHub Actions run for each project and shows it as passed, failed or unknown. Each card shows the last run's time, the branch and the commit.

It reads the results from GitHub each time, so it does not keep its own copy that could go out of date.

sections.heading: Decisions I made
sections.body:
I read the results from GitHub instead of storing them by hand. A hand-edited file would have been out of date as soon as a test ran.

Tests run on each push and pull request, and also on a timer, four times a day per project. The timed runs show whether a project is quiet or still working.

The layout is simple. The status and the last run sit in one panel, and the history stays in a corner.

sections.heading: What went wrong
sections.body:
The page asked GitHub for every project on every load. After about an hour, GitHub refused the requests, and every card showed unknown. A GitHub token fixed it.

A billing lock on my GitHub account made every run fail before any test ran. The dashboard showed those as broken tests, which made it look like my code was failing.

sections.heading: What I would do next
sections.body:
Show a clear message on the card when GitHub refuses a request, instead of unknown.

Run accessibility checks on this dashboard too. I have not done that yet, so I make no accessibility claims for it.

Count failures over the last 20 runs, so flaky tests are easy to spot.
